extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (practitioners of patent litigation and licensing)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of legal principles governing licenses, royalties, co-ownership, jurisdictional venue, government use, and abandonment/public use in patent law. Focused on remedies and defenses between contracting parties concerning patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty liability despite patent invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent is apparently valid and in force the party using it, receiving the benefit of its supposed validity, is liable for royalties agreed to be paid and cannot set up as a defence the actual invalidity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: party has got what he bargained for; cannot both affirm and disaffirm the patent; while manufacture goes on under an apparently valid patent it is presumed to be under and in accordance with the agreement to pay royalties. If manufacturer intends to act hostile to the patent (i.e., not under it), he must give notice of that intention. Cases and nuances: Milligan v. LaFrance; Marston v. Swett and others; differences where patent is annulled by judicial proceedings or priority awarded to others (then manufacture may be free).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repudiation/eviction required to defend on invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee must repudiate his license before he can defend against a claim for royalties by denying the validity of the patent; mere pleading that the patent is void is not of itself a sufficient defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that amounts to an 'eviction' (e.g., judicial annulment/destroying of the patent or discovery that exclusive title has been asserted by another) is sufficient to allow licensee to deny liability for further royalties. The difficulty lies in what constitutes eviction in patent context; courts examine whether licensee has actually been deprived of the benefit of the patent (see White v. Lee, Lewes v. Purser, and analogous cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of license does not relieve original licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of the license does not relieve the licensee from his obligation to pay the proper royalties; the assignee is regarded as his agent and the sales made on his account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Wilde v. Smith and similar cases. Also joint licensees are jointly and severally liable; a former member who acted as surety may still be pursued for fees paid on behalf of the firm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to pay royalties not equal to infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A failure to pay royalties does not make the licensee an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensee's contractual breach (non-payment) gives licensor remedies at law or in equity (damages, suit for fees), but does not automatically convert licensee's lawful exercise under the license into tortious infringement (see Consolidated Middlings Purifier Co. v. Wolf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party claims of infringement are not a defense to royalty suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere claim by third parties that the licensee infringes is no defence to an action for royalties on sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensee must show actual eviction or deprivation of the exclusive use (e.g., prior patentee supplying market asserting superior rights) to avoid royalties; mere allegations by third parties do not suffice (see Davis v. Gray and Angier v. Eaton, Cole & Bumham Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensor cannot enjoin licensee from exercising licensed rights for unpaid fees
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensor cannot prevent the licensee by injunction from exercising his rights under the license on the ground that license fees remain unpaid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensor's remedy for unpaid fees is by suit for damages or recovery of fees; equity may restrain certain conduct, but courts will not readily enjoin the licensee's exercise of agreed rights where the dispute is about fees (see cited cases and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits received by licensee bar challenge to validity in royalty suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a patent may not be good for all it claims, a licensee having the benefit of it cannot take advantage of its invalidity in a suit for royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where licensee has had all the benefit of a valid patent (e.g., kept off competition, exploited the market), courts hold he is liable for royalties despite some invalidity of specific claims. Exceptions exist where eviction/destruction of patent occurs or prior patent owner's superior title is established (cases vary; see Bartlett v. Holbrook and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensor's recourse when charging excessive fees
rubrics_metrics.description: If licensor charges more than agreed, his true defence is at law, but he may be enjoined from declaring the license void and thus putting the licensee to great loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable remedies may prevent licensor from repudiating the contract in a manner that causes disproportionate harm, even while monetary disputes proceed at law (see Baker Mfg. Co. v. Washburn & Moen Mfg. Co. and accompanying notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of joint patentees/co-owners (no implied mutual duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: No relation is created between joint-owners of a patent by the mere fact of their common interest in the invention; each is entitled to practise the invention and to license others without accountability to his co-owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a co-owner exceeds the privilege conferred and employs an infringing art or instrument, he is to his co-owners like a stranger and may be sued for infringement. Special contracts are necessary to create mutual responsibilities; such contracts are construed like ordinary contracts. Implied contracts may arise in certain circumstances (see §1253 and cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint patentees by re-issue may become inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee of an original invention and the inventor of an improvement unite in a re-issue covering the improved invention and are named as joint patentees, their rights may become inseparable and either can restrain the other from employing the invention except for their joint benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific factual situations (e.g., re-issue that merges interests) can change the default rule that co-owners act independently; see cited case law (e.g., Duke v. Graham and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-owners who are partners: patent rights subordinated to partnership
rubrics_metrics.description: When joint-owners are also partners in the business employing the patented invention, their rights as patentees are subordinated to their rights as partners; neither may use or license the invention contrary to the welfare of the common enterprise and may be enjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partnership purchasers in good faith without knowledge of the partnership agreement can still exercise privileges but leave remedy against the breaching partner for damages. Partnership agreements may require compensation (wages) for time devoted; such wages can be asserted as debts if no profits are realized. Partnership agreements are void if the patent is invalid; either partner can set up invalidity in defense to contract actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint licensees: joint and several liability and suretyship
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint licensees typically become jointly and severally liable to the licensor for performance and payment of stipulated fees; each member of the licensed firm is a surety for the collective obligations and may be held responsible for fulfilment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights and remedies among joint licensees follow ordinary partnership law; a licensee has remedy against the firm for payments made on its account. In actions to enforce these rights, liability of the surety or firm to the licensor is not open to inquiry, the surety being entitled to recovery if damnified (see Sizer v. Ray and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction over contract actions in patent context
rubrics_metrics.description: In actions upon contracts the jurisdiction of the Federal courts depends upon the citizenship of the parties, although the subject-matter is a right arising under the Patent Laws; when plaintiff and defendant reside in different States, such actions may be instituted in Federal courts; when parties are citizens of the same State, local tribunals alone have jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A State court cannot decree assignment of a patent on ground that petitioner is the true inventor (that adjudicates priority). Federal jurisdictional limits are emphasized; certain issues (priority/assignment) are for federal courts. See §1256 and cited authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts' jurisdiction over contract actions involving patents
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts have jurisdiction over pure contract questions even when patent validity or construction is collateral; they can compel specific performance, set aside agreements, award damages for breach of warranty, enforce payment of royalties, and enjoin torts/violations where adequate remedy at law is lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations: State courts cannot (ordinarily) adjudicate the existence of the patent as a federal franchise, cannot assign patents on ground of priority, and should not render judgments that affect the patent franchise. Nevertheless, State courts may pass on validity collaterally when relevant to contract issues (see Nichols v. Marsh, Continental Store Service Co. v. Clark, and numerous cases in §1257).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of Claims jurisdiction and government use compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court of Claims has jurisdiction over contract claims of individuals against the United States, and is the proper forum to seek compensation when the Government has used a patented invention without consent; jurisdiction historically limited as to torts but the court may entertain implied-contract claims for compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles: wrongful invasion by sovereign presumed to be under an implied contract to pay reasonable compensation; the U.S. may be liable for using the invention without license; officials cannot bind the U.S. by unauthorized contracts; damages measure may be the value of the invention to the government; Congress may direct references to determine compensation. See discussion of James v. Campbell, Palmer v. United States, Dahlgren, Hubbell, and other cases in §1258.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use nuances (liability and measure of damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the United States practises the invention without license it is liable to make compensation; where government uses but does not deal in the invention, damages are measured by the value of the invention to the government over other devices it had a right to employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court of Claims may have jurisdiction for royalties and implied-contract compensation; the U.S. is not liable for issuance of a patent to a rival inventor; government agents acting within duties may create use but cannot alone bind the nation to pay unless authorized; officers cannot claim royalties for using their own invention in public service. See numerous cited Ct. of Claims decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment to the public requires completed invention (mental conception insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere mental conception can be abandoned as to rival inventors, but only a completed invention can be abandoned to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere idea from reduced-to-practice/completed invention; see Webster v. Sanford and later cases (appendix entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in applying for patent: not automatically abandonment but risky
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay in applying for a patent is not ipso facto abandonment, but such delay may defeat the first inventor in favor of a diligent later inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law shows delay per se is not conclusive; courts examine diligence of competing inventors and intervening public uses (see United States Electric Lighting Co. v. Consolidated Electric Light Co.; Hubel v. Dick and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use vs public use (statutory bar considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental sale and use is not public use; an experimental use by an inventor is not public use even if profit is derived, but if the use is mainly for profit and the experiment incidental, and the use is public for more than two years before application, it constitutes abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where invention put into public use without reserving rights, exercising control, or examining to test efficiency, the use is not experimental. The burden rests on the patentee to show a public use more than two years before application was experimental (see Smith & Griggs Mfg. Co. v. Sprague; Root v. Third Ave. R.R. Co.; Campbell v. City of New York).
